title: Maker Lab: Robotics Adventure
description: Build your dream robot from scratch! Navigate the Maker Lab board, collect components, learn about electronics, coding, and mechanical design. Face engineering challenges, visit the parts shop, and compete against rival makers to build the best robot in the school science fair!
learning_objectives: Understand basic robotics components: sensors, motors, microcontrollers, and power systems
Learn about electronic circuits, programming logic, and mechanical design
Practice resource management and engineering trade-offs
Develop problem-solving skills through real-world STEM challenges
Explore the maker movement and hands-on learning culture

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: Roll the dice to move your maker avatar along the board from your Workbench to the Science Fair stage
Land on Engineering Challenge tiles to face decisions about your robot's design, coding, and components
Visit the Parts Shop to buy sensors, motors, and tools with your workshop budget
Beat the Technical Quiz tiles by answering STEM knowledge questions correctly
Race against AI rivals Anika and Dev to reach the Science Fair with the best-built robot
tips: Balance your spending between components (robot_quality) and tools (skills) -- both matter for the Science Fair
Keep team_spirit high -- your maker crew works better when motivated
Save budget for unexpected hardware failures -- soldering irons break at the worst times!
Technical Quiz tiles are your chance to gain big bonuses -- study your STEM basics

challenge.question: A judge at the science fair asks: What does the 'I' in IoT stand for?
challenge.success_message: Correct! Internet of Things -- you clearly know your tech fundamentals. The judge is impressed!
challenge.fail_message: Not quite! IoT stands for 'Internet of Things'. The judge suggests reading more about connected devices.
challenge.explanation: IoT stands for 'Internet of Things' -- the network of physical devices embedded with sensors, software, and connectivity that allows them to collect and exchange data over the internet. Examples include smart thermostats, fitness trackers, and connected home appliances. The 'Internet' in IoT is what distinguishes these devices from standalone electronics -- their ability to communicate and share data through the internet is what makes them 'smart'.

sensor_choice.title: Sensor Selection Dilemma
sensor_choice.description: Your robot needs to detect obstacles. You can use an ultrasonic sensor (reliable but basic) or an infrared sensor array (advanced but tricky to calibrate). A classmate offers their broken LIDAR sensor that you could try to repair.

choices.label: Use the reliable ultrasonic sensor
choices.feedback: Smart choice! The HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor sends sound pulses and measures echo time to detect obstacles up to 4 metres away. It's the go-to sensor for beginners and works perfectly for your robot.

choices.label: Try the advanced infrared array
choices.feedback: Ambitious! The IR array needs careful calibration but gives your robot the ability to detect obstacles at multiple angles simultaneously. You learned a lot about analog signal processing in the process.

choices.label: Attempt to repair the LIDAR
choices.feedback: The LIDAR was too damaged to use, but you learned incredible things about how laser-based distance measurement works! Your skills jumped up even though the robot quality took a small hit.

wiring_mess.title: Spaghetti Wiring Crisis
wiring_mess.description: Your robot's wiring looks like a plate of maggi noodles! Wires are tangled, some connections are loose, and the motor randomly jerks. You need to fix this before proceeding.

choices.label: Rewire everything neatly with cable ties
choices.feedback: Excellent! Clean wiring isn't just aesthetic -- it prevents short circuits, makes debugging easier, and impresses judges. You used cable ties, heat shrink tubing, and proper wire routing. Professional-grade work!

choices.label: Just tape down the loose connections
choices.feedback: Quick fix, but electrical tape over loose connections is a recipe for intermittent failures. Your team is frustrated because they know this will cause problems later.

choices.label: Use a PCB and solder connections properly
choices.feedback: The ultimate solution! Soldering connections onto a custom PCB makes your robot rock-solid. You learned about circuit board design, soldering technique, and why real products use PCBs instead of breadboards.

motor_test.title: Motor Testing Gone Wrong
motor_test.description: During testing, your robot's DC motor suddenly starts spinning at full speed and shoots across the room! The motor driver is sending the wrong PWM signal. What do you do?

choices.label: Debug the motor driver code line by line
choices.feedback: Methodical approach! You found that the PWM duty cycle was set to 255 (full speed) instead of 128 (half speed). You learned about Pulse Width Modulation -- how rapidly switching a signal on/off controls motor speed. Fixing the code taught you valuable debugging skills.

choices.label: Replace with a slower motor and gear system
choices.feedback: A gear reduction system trades speed for torque, giving your robot more control and power. The 1:48 gear ratio means the wheel turns once for every 48 motor rotations -- slow but steady and strong!

choices.label: Add a hardware speed limiter circuit
choices.feedback: Smart hardware solution! You built a voltage divider and a potentiometer circuit to limit the maximum voltage reaching the motor. Even if the code bugs out, the hardware prevents dangerous speeds. Defence in depth!

code_bug.title: The Infinite Loop Bug
code_bug.description: Your robot's Arduino code compiles fine, but when you upload it, the robot just spins in circles endlessly! The serial monitor shows 'Turning left...' repeating forever. Classic infinite loop bug!

choices.label: Add a counter to limit loop iterations
choices.feedback: Adding a counter variable that breaks the loop after 10 iterations fixed the spinning. But the real lesson is: always have exit conditions in your loops! while(true) is dangerous without a break statement.

choices.label: Rewrite the navigation logic from scratch
choices.feedback: A complete rewrite using a proper state machine pattern. Your robot now has states: FORWARD, TURN_LEFT, TURN_RIGHT, STOP. Each state has clear entry/exit conditions. Much more robust code, but your team was stressed by the extra work.

choices.label: Ask the coding club teacher for help
choices.feedback: The teacher showed you how to use the Serial Monitor for debugging and explained that the sensor was returning -1 (error) which your code interpreted as 'obstacle on right, turn left forever'. You learned about error handling and your team appreciates the mentor's guidance.

3d_print_fail.title: 3D Print Catastrophe
3d_print_fail.description: Your robot chassis was printing overnight and you arrive to find a spaghetti mess of filament! The print failed halfway through. The science fair is in 3 days.

choices.label: Re-print with better settings (slower, more support)
choices.feedback: Patience pays off! You lowered the print speed from 60mm/s to 30mm/s, added supports for overhangs, and increased bed adhesion with a brim. The second print came out perfectly. Lesson: faster isn't always better in manufacturing!

choices.label: Build a chassis from cardboard and hot glue
choices.feedback: The cardboard chassis isn't pretty but it works! Hot glue, craft paper, and creativity saved the day. Many award-winning maker projects start with cardboard prototypes. Function over form!

choices.label: Laser-cut an acrylic chassis at the fab lab
choices.feedback: The fab lab's laser cutter produced a gorgeous acrylic chassis in 20 minutes! You learned about CAD design, kerf compensation, and the difference between additive (3D printing) and subtractive (laser cutting) manufacturing.

team_conflict.title: Team Disagreement: Design vs Code
team_conflict.description: Your team's hardware person and software person are arguing! The hardware person wants to add more sensors, but the coder says the Arduino doesn't have enough memory for more sensor code. They're not talking to each other.

choices.label: Mediate and find a technical compromise
choices.feedback: Great leadership! You suggested using an Arduino Mega (more pins and memory) and prioritising the 3 most important sensors. Both team members felt heard and the solution was better than either original idea.

choices.label: Side with the hardware person -- more sensors!
choices.feedback: More sensors mean better obstacle detection, but the coder is demotivated. The code became buggy because it was rushed to accommodate all the hardware. Team harmony is as important as technical decisions.

choices.label: Side with the coder -- optimise the software first
choices.feedback: Optimised code is powerful -- your coder wrote efficient interrupt-based sensor reading that actually works better with fewer sensors. But the hardware person felt sidelined. Consider both perspectives next time.

team_conflict.reflection_prompt: When two teammates disagree, a leader must decide whether to mediate, pick a side, or step back. Think about a time you were caught between two people who both had good points. How did you handle it? Did you prioritize the relationship or the outcome? What does your instinct in these moments reveal about your leadership style?

power_supply.title: Power Supply Problem
power_supply.description: Your robot runs fine for 2 minutes, then the motors slow down and the Arduino resets. The 9V battery can't provide enough current for motors + sensors + the microcontroller simultaneously!

choices.label: Switch to a LiPo battery pack
choices.feedback: Lithium Polymer batteries are the gold standard for robotics! They deliver high current, are rechargeable, and pack serious energy density. Your robot now runs for 30+ minutes at full power. Just be careful -- LiPo batteries need proper charging circuits to be safe.

choices.label: Use separate power sources for motors and logic
choices.feedback: Engineer's solution! You used a 4xAA battery pack (6V) for motors and a USB power bank for the Arduino. This also prevents motor noise from resetting the microcontroller. You learned about power rail isolation -- a real-world engineering technique!

choices.label: Reduce power consumption with sleep modes
choices.feedback: Software optimisation for hardware problems! You programmed the Arduino to put sensors into sleep mode when not in use, and duty-cycle the motors (pulse rather than constant run). Your battery life tripled and you learned about embedded systems power management.

competition_spy.title: Rival Team's Impressive Robot
competition_spy.description: You sneak a peek at Dev's robot and it looks incredible -- it has a robotic arm, colour sensor, and a custom app controlling it via Bluetooth! Your team feels discouraged.

choices.label: Focus on your own strengths and keep building
choices.feedback: Wise choice! Comparison is the thief of joy. Your robot may not have a Bluetooth app, but its obstacle avoidance is solid and reliable. Judges value working functionality over flashy features that might fail during the demo.

choices.label: Add a Bluetooth module to your robot too
choices.feedback: Adding Bluetooth (HC-05 module) gave your robot app control, but the rush to implement it meant the connection is unreliable. Sometimes it's better to perfect core features than to chase feature parity with competitors.

choices.label: Pivot to something unique -- add a gripper arm
choices.feedback: Differentiation! Instead of copying Dev's features, you built a simple servo-powered gripper arm that picks up objects. This unique feature will stand out to judges who see many similar robots. Innovation beats imitation!

competition_spy.reflection_prompt: Seeing a rival's impressive work can be motivating or demoralizing. How do you usually react when someone else seems to be doing better than you? Do you compare yourself and feel discouraged, or do you use it as fuel to improve? What strategies help you stay focused on your own progress?

sponsor_visit.title: Tech Company Sponsor Visit
sponsor_visit.description: A local tech company is visiting the school to sponsor the science fair. They'll give bonus equipment to the team with the best pitch about their project. How do you prepare?

choices.label: Create a detailed technical presentation
choices.feedback: Your technical presentation impressed the sponsors! You explained your robot's architecture, the challenges you faced, and how you solved them. They donated a sensor kit and sponsored your team's materials. Communication skills matter as much as building skills!

choices.label: Do a live demo of your robot in action
choices.feedback: The live demo was exciting! Your robot navigated an obstacle course and the team cheered when it completed it. The sponsors loved the energy and gave you components. Remember: showing is more powerful than telling.

choices.label: Show your project documentation and code repository
choices.feedback: The sponsors were impressed by your GitHub repository, wiring diagrams, and build log. They said 'This is how real engineers work.' You got a modest sponsorship but earned their respect. Documentation is an underrated skill.

shortcut_hack.title: The Shortcut Temptation
shortcut_hack.description: You found a pre-made robot kit online that looks exactly like what you're building. For Rs 2000, you could buy it and claim you built it from scratch. Nobody would know... or would they?

choices.label: Absolutely not -- keep building from scratch
choices.feedback: Integrity wins! The whole point of the maker movement is learning by building. Your handmade robot might have flaws, but every flaw taught you something. The judges can tell the difference between someone who bought a kit and someone who really understands their robot.

choices.label: Buy the kit for reference but build your own
choices.feedback: Studying the kit's design without copying it is legitimate learning! You reverse-engineered the motor mounting system and adapted it for your robot. Engineers study existing products all the time -- it's called 'competitive analysis'.

choices.label: Buy just the wheels and structural parts
choices.feedback: A practical compromise. The precision-machined wheels and metal brackets are better than anything you could make by hand. Using off-the-shelf components for non-critical parts while building the core yourself is what real engineers do.

shortcut_hack.reflection_prompt: The temptation to take a shortcut tests your integrity when nobody is watching. Have you ever been in a situation where you could have taken credit for work you did not do, or used someone else's work as your own? What stopped you -- or what would you do differently? What is the real cost of shortcuts beyond getting caught?

design_review.title: Design Review with the Teacher
design_review.description: Your science teacher reviews your robot design and points out that the centre of gravity is too high -- your robot will tip over when turning fast. How do you fix it?

choices.label: Lower the battery placement to the base
choices.feedback: Physics in action! Moving the heaviest component (battery) to the lowest point dramatically improves stability. This is the same principle that keeps racing cars low to the ground. Your robot now handles sharp turns without toppling.

choices.label: Add wider wheels for a broader base
choices.feedback: A wider wheelbase increases the base of support, making the robot more stable. It's a trade-off though -- wider robots need more turning radius. You learned about the stability triangle concept used in forklift design.

choices.label: Reduce turning speed in software
choices.feedback: Software solution! You added acceleration curves to the motor control so the robot gradually speeds up turns instead of jerking. This prevents tipping and makes movement smoother. Sometimes the fix isn't hardware -- it's algorithm design.

open_source.title: Open Source Discovery
open_source.description: You found an open-source robotics library on GitHub that has amazing obstacle avoidance code. It's free to use but you'll need to understand and modify it for your robot.

choices.label: Fork it and learn from the code
choices.feedback: The open-source community is incredible! You forked the repository, read through the code, and understood how PID controllers work for smooth motor control. You adapted the obstacle avoidance algorithm for your specific sensors. This is how real developers work!

choices.label: Use it as-is without modification
choices.feedback: It works, but you don't fully understand the code. When a judge asks 'How does your obstacle avoidance work?', you struggle to explain. Using open-source is fine, but understanding what you use is essential.

choices.label: Write your own algorithm inspired by it
choices.feedback: Reading the open-source code inspired you to write your own version! It's not as sophisticated, but you understand every line. Your team feels proud that the code is 100% yours. The judges will appreciate your genuine understanding.

battery_crisis.title: Battery Emergency on Demo Day
battery_crisis.description: It's the morning of the science fair and your LiPo battery is dead! You forgot to charge it last night. The fair starts in 2 hours.

choices.label: Rush to the electronics shop for a new battery
choices.feedback: Crisis management! You sprinted to the nearest electronics shop and bought a compatible battery. The extra cost hurt, but your robot will have full power for the demo. Lesson learned: always have a pre-event checklist!

choices.label: Use AA batteries as an emergency backup
choices.feedback: Your team jerry-rigged 6 AA batteries into a holder. The voltage is slightly lower so motors are slower, but your robot works! The team's creative problem-solving under pressure is impressive. Adaptability is a maker superpower.

choices.label: Charge for 1 hour and hope it's enough
choices.feedback: A partial charge gives you about 15 minutes of runtime -- enough for the demo if you're efficient. You planned a shorter demonstration that focuses on your robot's best features. Time management under pressure!

final_test.title: Final Testing Before the Fair
final_test.description: Last chance to test your robot! You can do a careful test run in the classroom, stress-test it on a difficult obstacle course, or spend the time polishing the presentation instead.

choices.label: Careful test run and fix any small issues
choices.feedback: Methodical testing revealed a loose wire and a sensor calibration issue. Both easy fixes that would have caused embarrassing failures during the actual demo. Testing is the most important phase of any engineering project!

choices.label: Extreme stress test on a hard obstacle course
choices.feedback: Your robot survived a gauntlet of ramps, tight corners, and moving obstacles! One wheel came loose under stress, so you reinforced it. Stress testing reveals hidden weaknesses. Your team is confident the robot can handle anything the judges throw at it.

choices.label: Skip testing and perfect the presentation
choices.feedback: Your presentation slides and speech are polished and professional. But skipping the final test meant you didn't catch a motor alignment issue that causes your robot to drift left. Testing should never be sacrificed for presentation prep.

sensors.definition: Devices that detect physical properties like light, temperature, or distance and convert them into signals a robot can process.
sensors.example: An ultrasonic sensor measures distance by sending sound waves and timing the echo.
sensors.real_world_example: Self-driving cars use LiDAR sensors to create 3D maps of their surroundings in real-time.

actuators.definition: Components that convert energy into physical motion — the "muscles" of a robot. Include motors, servos, and hydraulics.
actuators.example: A servo motor that rotates a robot arm to pick up objects.
actuators.real_world_example: Industrial robots in car factories use precise actuators to weld, paint, and assemble vehicles.

programming_logic.definition: The use of conditional statements (if/else), loops, and sequences to control robot behavior and decision-making.
programming_logic.example: If distance_sensor < 30cm then turn_right else go_forward.
programming_logic.real_world_example: Roomba vacuum robots use programming logic to navigate rooms, avoid stairs, and return to their charging dock.

ai_robotics.definition: Using artificial intelligence to give robots the ability to learn, adapt, and make decisions without explicit programming.
ai_robotics.example: A robot learning to grasp objects of different shapes through trial and error.
ai_robotics.real_world_example: Boston Dynamics' Atlas robot uses AI to maintain balance while running, jumping, and doing backflips.

mechanical_design.definition: The engineering process of designing physical structures, joints, and mechanisms that allow robots to move and interact.
mechanical_design.example: Designing a gripper with opposing fingers that can hold objects of various sizes.
mechanical_design.real_world_example: The Mars Perseverance rover's mechanical arm has 5 joints and 7 motors, designed to drill rock samples.

win_criteria.label: Best Resource Balance
win_criteria.description: Lowest variance across all resource growth percentages

transfer_exercises.game_context: Navigating resource trade-offs on the board
transfer_exercises.real_world: Managing a project budget with competing priorities
transfer_exercises.challenge: List 3 real decisions you made this week that involved trade-offs between short-term and long-term outcomes.

transfer_exercises.game_context: Taking bold moves despite uncertain outcomes
transfer_exercises.real_world: Starting a new initiative at school or work without guaranteed success
transfer_exercises.challenge: Identify one situation where you played it too safe. What would you try differently?

glossary_terms.definition: Placing yourself or your resources in a location that gives future advantages.
glossary_terms.example: Investing in infrastructure early allows faster growth in later rounds.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Good positioning is proactive, not reactive — you set up future wins before the opportunity arises.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Companies open offices in growing cities before competition arrives, securing better talent and costs.

glossary_terms.definition: The skillful allocation of limited assets (money, time, staff) to maximize results.
glossary_terms.example: Deciding whether to spend your limited budget on defense or expansion this turn.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Effective resource management requires prioritization — not every goal can be pursued simultaneously.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Project managers balance budget, time, and team capacity to deliver results on schedule.

glossary_terms.definition: When growth builds upon previous growth, creating accelerating returns over time.
glossary_terms.example: A small investment in customer experience leads to word-of-mouth, which brings more customers.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Compound growth requires patience — early results seem small, but the acceleration becomes dramatic over time.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Interest in savings accounts compounds: ₹1000 at 10% becomes ₹1610 in 5 years, not just ₹1500.
